title: Why memory got wider but not closer
objective: By the end of this lesson you can convert a CAS latency in cycles into nanoseconds, explain why that number has barely moved across five generations, and say what a faster memory generation actually buys.

blocks.text: Memory generations are marketed by their data rate: DDR4-3200, DDR5-6400, and so on. That number has grown enormously. The number that governs how long a single dependent load waits has not, and the gap between the two is one of the defining facts of modern performance.

blocks.title: The most common mistake in memory shopping
blocks.text: DDR4 modules commonly carry CL16 to CL22 and DDR5 modules CL32 to CL46, which reads as a large regression if you compare the numbers directly. Convert them and the picture changes completely: the cycles got roughly twice as short, so twice as many of them take about the same time. Always convert to nanoseconds before comparing anything across generations.

Turn the question around. Instead of looking up what CL each generation shipped with, ask what CL each would need in order to deliver the same 14 nanoseconds — a figure the DDR5 documentation itself gives as roughly unchanged from DDR3 and DDR4.

blocks.caption: Computed, not looked up
lines: For a first-word latency of 14 ns, what CAS latency in CYCLES is required?
/* Peak transfer multiplied by 22. The CL numbers multiplied by 22 as well
-- and the time they represent did not move. Those computed CL values
are close to the ones real modules of each generation carry, which is
what makes the flat-latency claim checkable rather than merely repeated. */

blocks.text: Peak transfer rate rose by a factor of twenty-two. The latency stayed put. This is not an oversight: latency is dominated by the physics of sensing a tiny charge and driving a signal across a board, and neither improves when the interface runs faster. Transfer rate is a matter of how quickly bits can be pushed down a wire once the row is open, and that has improved enormously.
What a new generation actually buys

headers: Improves little or not at all
rows: A pointer chase through a linked structure
Serving many independent requests at once
One dependent load waiting for another
A cache miss on a critical path

blocks.text: The left column is throughput and the right is latency — the same distinction the pipelining module drew, appearing again at the level of the memory system. A faster memory generation is a throughput improvement, so it helps code shaped like the left column and does almost nothing for code shaped like the right.

blocks.title: This is why cache design keeps getting more elaborate
blocks.text: If main memory latency will not improve, the only remaining way to reduce the average cost of an access is to reach main memory less often. That is the entire justification for multi-level caches, larger caches, more sophisticated prefetchers, and speculative execution. The whole edifice this course has described exists because one number stopped improving decades ago and never resumed.

rows: 4800 MT/s and up, to 8800 in the current standard

blocks.text: The voltage column tells its own story: each generation moves more data while using less energy per bit, which is what makes the higher rates thermally possible at all. The DDR5 standard was published in July 2020 and its maximum defined data rate was raised to 8800 MT/s in the JESD79-5C revision of April 2024, so the top of that range is a moving target — check the current standard rather than a remembered figure.

blocks.title: Convert and compare
steps: Find the memory specification of a machine you own
Write down its data rate and CAS latency in cycles
Convert the CL to nanoseconds using CL / clock in MHz x 1000
Compare that number with the 14 ns figure quoted here
Now measure it: run the random pointer chase from the previous lesson at a working set far larger than your cache
Compare your measured latency with the CL you computed and explain the gap
List three things included in the measured number that CL does not cover
State what fraction of your measured latency the CL actually accounts for
blocks.expected: A measured latency substantially larger than the computed CL — on the machine used in this module, 188 ns measured against a CL of roughly 14 ns. The gap is the point: CL is one step of many, and the rest is address translation, cache lookups at every level, the row open and close, queueing in the memory controller, and the trip across the board. Quoting CL as 'memory latency' understates the real figure by an order of magnitude.

cheatsheet: Data rate in MT/s is twice the clock in MHz, because DDR transfers on both edges
latency in ns = CL / clock in MHz x 1000
A larger CL number does not mean slower memory; the cycles are shorter
Computed: holding 14 ns fixed requires CL 2.8 at DDR-400 and CL 61.6 at DDR5-8800
Peak transfer rose about 22x across those generations while latency stayed flat
A new generation is a throughput improvement, not a latency one
It helps streaming and many parallel requests; it barely helps a pointer chase
Flat memory latency is the reason cache hierarchies keep growing more elaborate
Measured full latency was 188 ns against a CL of about 14 ns — CL is one step of many

checkpoint.prompt: DDR5-6400 has a clock of 3200 MHz and CL46. What is the first-word latency?
checkpoint.explanation: CL divided by the clock in MHz, times 1000. The data rate 6400 MT/s is twice the clock because DDR transfers on both clock edges.

checkpoint.prompt: DDR4 modules commonly carry CL16-22 and DDR5 modules CL32-46. Has memory latency roughly doubled?

choices.C: No — the cycles are about half as long

checkpoint.explanation: Roughly twice as many of them take about the same time. Comparing CL across generations without converting to nanoseconds compares counts of different-sized units. Convert first, always.

checkpoint.prompt: Peak transfer rate rose roughly 22x from DDR-400 to DDR5-8800 while latency stayed near 14 ns. Which code benefits most from the newer generation?

choices.A: Code dominated by one cache miss on the critical path
choices.C: Streaming through large arrays and serving many independent requests at once

checkpoint.explanation: A faster generation is a throughput improvement. The same latency-versus-throughput distinction from the pipelining module, applied to the memory system.

checkpoint.prompt: Why is measured memory latency around 188 ns when CL is about 14 ns?

choices.C: CL is one step among many
choices.D: CL is quoted at a different clock

checkpoint.explanation: Address translation, cache lookups at every level, opening and closing the row, controller queueing and the trip across the board are all included in the measured figure. Quoting CL as 'memory latency' understates the real cost by roughly an order of magnitude, which is why the measurement and the specification must both be understood.
